query: Starting from a eutectic high-entropy alloy with a hierarchical microstructure of dual-phase lamellar colonies, what single intervention could overcome limited room-temperature tensile ductility and brittleness while retaining or increasing strength? The hypothesis should address the tendency for dislocation pile-ups near internal boundaries to produce local stress concentrations, microcracking, and catastrophic damage during straining. Specify the intervention, its mechanism, the predicted strength and ductility relative to the untreated starting material, the applicable testing and operating conditions, supporting prior evidence, and a falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: A short-duration partial solution anneal near the eutectic temperature (e.g., 1150–1200 °C) followed by moderate-temperature aging (around 600–700 °C) will refine lamellar spacing, improve interfacial coherence, and reduce dislocation pile-ups in a eutectic high-entropy alloy’s dual-phase colonies, thereby increasing room-temperature tensile ductility while retaining or slightly increasing strength.
generation.material_initial_state: As-cast or as-solidified eutectic high-entropy alloy with a dual-phase lamellar microstructure prone to dislocation pile-ups and brittleness under tensile loading.
generation.intervention: Thermal treatment comprising a short partial solution anneal near the eutectic temperature, followed by a moderate-temperature aging step of several hours.
generation.conditions: Standard room-temperature uniaxial tensile tests on samples processed under the described annealing and aging conditions.
generation.structural_mediator: Refined, semi-coherent lamellar interfaces that allow more uniform dislocation motion across phase boundaries and reduce local stress concentrations.
generation.mechanism: Partial solution annealing disrupts coarse lamellar boundaries and drives partial dissolution of the harder phase, while subsequent aging re-precipitates nanoscale particles to strengthen the matrix. These processed boundaries and precipitates facilitate dislocation transfer through colony interfaces and mitigate stress concentrations, reducing microcracking.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the untreated material, ductility will be noticeably higher (potentially 20–30% improvement in elongation), while yield and ultimate tensile strengths will be retained or slightly increased due to refined precipitation and improved boundary cohesion.
generation.baseline: Untreated eutectic HEA lamellar colonies experience significant dislocation pile-ups at interfaces, leading to early crack initiation and limited elongation (often <5–10%), coupled with high strength but poor tensile ductility at room temperature.
generation.boundary: Excessively long or high-temperature solution anneals may cause unwanted grain coarsening or over-dissolution of strengthening phases, compromising both ductility and strength. Optimal parameters likely depend on specific alloy composition.
generation.uncertainty: Exact annealing times, temperatures, and resulting mechanical property gains may differ depending on alloy composition and specific lamellar morphology, so further trials are needed to optimize parameters.

falsification_experiment.design: Conduct parallel processing trials of identical alloy melts: (1) partial solution anneal plus aging (test), (2) only solution anneal without aging, and (3) no heat treatment. Compare mechanical properties, dislocation substructure, and fracture surfaces in room-temperature tensile tests.
measurements: Tensile yield strength and elongation at room temperature
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If, under the prescribed heat treatment, dislocation pile-ups and microcracking at interfaces persist to the same degree as in the untreated material, and ductility is not measurably improved, the hypothesis is falsified.

Through TEM observations, we carefully characterized the evolution of the microstructure to discern the salient strengthening mechanisms generated by the SCCPs structure. Dislocation behavior at strains of 4%, 10%, and 14% in the W-based refractory HEA with the SCCPs structure are shown in Fig. 4 . Figure 4a–c, e reveal that dislocations cut through the δ-lamellae, yet are pinned by the γ ″ particles. For the coherent δ-lamellae structure, as the tensile stress increases up to the yield stress, dislocation slip occurs in the fcc matrix and involves shearing across the δ-lamellae, which indicates an early stage of the planar dislocation slip across the coherent δ/γ boundaries (Fig. 4a ). With further increase in strain to 10%, slip bands can clearly be observed across the δ-lamellae (Fig. 4b ). At a strain of 14%, shearing of the δ-lamellae by the slip bands leads to a large local shear (~40%) (Fig. 4c ), rather than the creation of a crack, which alleviates the local stress concentration. A schematic diagram of the interaction of dislocations with δ-lamellae is shown in Fig. 4d .

Refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) are a relatively new class of multicomponent materials that are based on several refractory metals, but may also contain other, generally low density, elements and typically have a body centered cubic (BCC) crystal structure [1] – [3] . These alloys have recently received much attention because of their attractive combination of properties not achievable by other classes of metallic alloys. For example, the first two RHEAs, NbMoTaW and NbMoTaVW, showed weak temperature dependence of yield strength in the temperature range from 600 °C to 1600 °C, with yield strength above 400 MPa at 1600 °C [4] , [5] . Unfortunately, these two alloys had high density (>12 g/cm 3 ) and further developments aimed at reducing the alloy density while keeping superior high-temperature properties. In the second generation RHEAs, high-density Ta and W were replaced with lower density refractory elements, such as Cr, Mo, Nb, V and Zr, and low density Al and Ti were added [6] – [13] . decision.trend: Early work (PMC4145285) on an as-cast eutectic high-entropy alloy with a lamellar fcc/B2 microstructure demonstrated balanced strength-ductility, though still prone to local boundary stresses. Subsequent studies (PMC5995863) showed that transforming a brittle B2 matrix into a fine-scale BCC/B2 mixture via solutionizing and aging raised ductility without sacrificing strength. Later efforts (PMC10213035) emphasized tailoring coherent precipitates and lamellar structures through careful thermo-mechanical schedules, enabling ultrahigh strength with moderate ductility. Yet fully mitigating boundary-induced microcracking under room-temperature tensile loads remains unachieved.
decision.unsolved: A consistent strategy to prevent dislocation pile-ups at colony or interphase boundaries and thereby avoid localized microcracks is lacking. The challenge is to refine or disrupt lamellar interfaces while retaining or boosting overall strength.
decision.lever: Short-duration partial solution annealing near the eutectic temperature (e.g. 1150–1200 °C), followed by a moderate-temperature aging (600–700 °C for several hours) to refine lamella spacing and promote slip continuity at colony boundaries.
decision.why: Such a two-step heat treatment has proven effective (PMC5995863, PMC10213035) in reducing stress concentrations at phase interfaces by introducing a more uniform, semi-coherent boundary network that hinders pile-ups. This mechanism should raise strength through fine-scale precipitation strengthening and enhance ductility by easing dislocation transfer across internal interfaces, as validated by room-temperature tensile tests. A falsification would involve omitting or varying the short solution anneal or aging time to confirm that unrefined lamellar boundaries persistently trigger early cracking.
